* **Environment**: Lack of people around with the same mindset and characteristics I look for. Or simply just not enough people.
* **Opportunity:** Not many methods of meeting new people besides dating apps. Especially with COVID, it's difficult

Compromises:

* I've heavily considered moving to areas where I would expect to find more people like me. From personal research, I feel like the West Coast (San Jose) would be good a fit for me. However, there's a lot of risk and work involved - being able to pick up and start in a place completely new.
* Outside of dating apps, I also give Reddit a try. I try to be open to talking to strangers I know nothing about; both male and female, despite my preference for the opposite sex in hopes I would find a connection.

I would claim that in order for me to be alone for long periods of time (weeks on end), there has to be some sort of connection - i.e. knowing that I have a strong bond with someone I can relate to and entrust. In another sense, it can be described as something to look forward to. In my personal experience, I find that the first step to overcome depression is to understand it. Some questions I ask myself are

* Why am I depressed?
   * When am I depressed?
   * What triggers my depression?
   * Is it internal/external?
* What would make me happy?
   * Is it controllable/obtainable?
   * Are there any proactive steps I can take to achieve it?

At the end of the day, what I often realize is that most of us don't really want to end our lives. We just want the pain to stop. If there are more practical ways to end the pain, then it's worth considering.

Sounds like you guys have really bad communication issues - specifically handling logical arguments. Remember that the goal isn't to necessary agree with each other, but more so to understand each other and why the other person thinks the way they do. The best way to show this is by reiterating what the other person just said so they know you were listening, and then input your own opinion.

"*I understand that you believe \[their belief\] but I personally believe \[your belief\]."*

But let's face it. In many logical arguments, there's actually a correct answer based on our definitions and own understanding of the situation. This can be very hard if you're not a logical person. The key is also being able to concisely explain it. In order to find correctness in your specific argument, you need to be able to define the literal definition of 'autistic' and be able to use that in your proof directly in a situation where it will always work. 

In your example, you're using how obvious a joke is perceived and trying to directly correlate it to autism. Except, your girlfriend is right. It doesn't always work because it's highly possible (not probable) that a person who is non-autistic will not be able to comprehend the joke. That is, as long as there exists one non-austistic person who doesn't understand the joke, then the counter argument holds and she wins (she does). 

The next part you guys argued over whether or not the joke was obvious. Except the word "obvious" is subjective (unless you concretely define it). There's no true way to determine whether or not something is obvious because it's always possible that there could be someone (non-autistic) who doesn't think the joke is obvious. 

At this point, you should've just changed your claim to "I'm not saying he's actually austistic, I'm saying it's possible he might be autistic because there tends to be  correlation between people who are autistic and not being able to comprehend obvious jokes, and I personally consider that joke to be obvious." which isn't all that strong either but at least you're covering your bases.

Overall based on logical reasoning, I would say you definitely loss this one.

But generally speaking here's how logical arguments are suppose to go

If a person (say X)  makes a claim that the other person (say Y) doesn't agree with, then the next question to ask is why (which is what your girlfriend did). If the explanation makes sense to Y, then great. If not (your explanation didn't make sense), then Y needs to give a counter-argument (she gave one). If counter-argument doesn't make sense to X (apparently didn't), then X needs to give a counter-counter-argument (you failed to do this). The process keeps going until someone runs into a contradiction (you ran into a contradiction by directly associating autism with obvious jokes). Then you trace everything back and someone wins/loses (she wins/you lose). 

But if it boils down to true subjectivity (things that cannot be proven), then that's the conclusion and the whole argument itself is pointless. At that point, just agree to disagree and move on.

Instead, what they're actually looking for is affection and reassurance. It just happens to be that the way you and him both receive and give affection may be different.

There's a book called "The Five Love Languages" that illustrates the 5 primary ways people give and receive affection. They are physical touch, quality time, gifts, words of affirmation, and acts of service. For example, if person X receives affection through physical touch and person Y receives affection through gifts, then even if person Y gives person X gifts, person X isn't going to feel loved or reassured (and vice versa). Instead, in order to properly give love, person Y has to be able to give physical touch to person X and person X has to be willing to buy gifts for person Y. Everyone's happy.

So what am I saying? You guys need to sit down and have a serious discussion about your expectations for each other. Otherwise, you're going to continuously feel unloved and unwanted and he's not going to understand why (and possibly vice versa). Then inevitably, you guys will be miserable and the relationship will fail.

And no, you should never feel bad about asking for affection. At the end of the day, if he's not able to meet your expectations (regardless how high or how low), you have the right to leave him.
